question: Virtual currencies used in video games, such as Robux from the Roblox game, are used to buy objects, enhancements for avatars or other features within the games themselves. However, the currencies can also be acquired with real money and used in the game concerned, or on other sites and in other games.

These currencies thus involve the malicious manipulation of minors, but they are also a financial burden for parents. For this reason, in the US, complaints have been made against the companies that operate the games. The complaints focus mainly on the dearth of adequate measures to protect minors.
In the EU, however, criticism is centred on the shortcomings of the Digital Services Act, which could, if necessary, be complemented by a digital fairness act. 1.

Rather than relying on possible self-regulation by the industry or additional European regulation, why not ban – within our internal market – these virtual currencies that are being used in video games and that are dangerous and addictive for minors?
Additionally, do these currencies not allow companies from third countries to gain an unfair advantage over their European competitors?
Supporters1
This question is supported by Members other than the author: Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE), Valérie Deloge (PfE).
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (17.3.2026) The protection of minors is a key priority for the Commission. Its Guidelines on the protection of minors online under the Digital Services Act (DSA)1 are clear: providers of online platforms should ensure that children are not exposed to techniques which can reduce transparency of economic transactions and may be misleading for minors.

In that context, the Guidelines give as an example certain virtual currencies2. Further, Article 25 DSA bars the use of interfaces that deceive or manipulate recipients3. While not all video games fall within the definition of online platforms under the DSA4, other legal instruments exist to protect minors online, such as the consumer protection or data protection acquis5.

Providers of video games have to adhere to the existing legal framework if they use virtual currencies. The Commission is in continuous exchanges with other regulators to take stock of the implementation of the existing rules. The Commission moreover considers that regulatory measures should be complemented, e.g. via awareness raising activities to help minors to attain improved digital literacy.

In this regard, the Commission has adopted a European strategy for a Better Internet for Kids (BIK+)6. Virtual currencies, which are common in video games, are equally used by EU and non-EU companies, reflecting this market being global by default.

In the context of the preparation of the upcoming Digital Fairness Act the Commission is exploring how to address problematic features in digital products such as social media, video games and e-commerce, in particular as concerns their impact on minors.
1 Regulation (EU) 2022/2065. 2 See Guidelines on measures to ensure a high level of privacy, safety and security for minors online, pursuant to

Article 28(4) of Regulation (EU) 2022/2065, (C/2025/5519), paragraph 69. 3 In this regard the DSA complements Directive 2005/29/EC or Regulation (EU) 2016/679. 4 Article 3(i) of Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 stipulates that a hosting service is, in general, an online platform if it stores and disseminates information to the public at the request of a recipient of the service.

5 See the Consumer Protection Cooperation Network’s Key Principles on In-game Virtual Currencies, https://commission.europa.eu/document/8af13e88-6540-436c-b137-9853e7fe866a_en. 6 See in particular regarding video games the AdWiseOnline 2025 initiative: https://better-internet-forkids.europa.eu/en/adwiseonline.
